content: Allicin is a potent compound with antibacterial and antifungal properties, derived from garlic. It is the primary chemical responsible for the pungent, hot, and burning taste characteristic of fresh garlic. However, allicin does not naturally exist in intact garlic. When garlic is chopped, crushed, or otherwise physically damaged, an enzymatic reaction occurs. The enzyme alliinase acts on a precursor compound called alliin, converting it into allicin. It is important to note that alliin is an amino acid that does not contribute to protein synthesis. Allicin is chemically unstable. It degrades gradually when left to stand and is rapidly destroyed when exposed to heat during cooking. Despite its instability, allicin has several medicinal applications. It has been shown to aid in combating arteriosclerosis by potentially improving vascular health. Additionally, it exhibits the ability to dissolve fats and serves as a mild antioxidant, offering some protection against oxidative stress.
